verdicts.trueWording: The entire bit about the wet shoes is left out
verdicts.note: Raw PDF via DSpace REST bitstream (item 2d2909fb, 45pp). Every limb holds: Duits quotes Hobb's 'My wet shoes were a misery' (AA 323) against Feberwee and Cuijpers's Dutch (246), which drops it. Cite drift only: the quoted sentence sits on printed p.17, its Hobb/Dutch setup on p.16; section 6 is correct.

verdicts.trueWording: According to Stableford, Hobb's novels are elaborately detailed
verdicts.note: Verbatim with the (200) page cite intact. The illustration limb holds: Duits writes that an example is the passage where Fitz reaches the Mountain Kingdom and sees the Chyurda, the Mountain people, for the first time. Printed p.6, section 2, both as cited.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the description ends on the fine-furs clause — one further sentence closes the block quote after it
verdicts.trueWording: They strode alongside us, mounted as we were
verdicts.note: The quoted words are verbatim on printed p.6 (full form: wore fine furs as if they were no more than homespun, Hobb 383). But the furs clause is second-to-last, not last: the block quote closes with the striding sentence above, ending 'no difficulty keeping up with the horses all day.' Use 'ends on' only of the Chyurda's dress, not of the passage.

verdicts.trueWording: Leerling en Meester is written in quite archaic language
verdicts.note: Verbatim, with the Dutch title named in the same sentence. Cite drift only: printed p.4, not p.3; section 1 Introduction (pp.3-4) is correct.

verdicts.trueWording: The word order seems unnatural as well
verdicts.note: Verbatim, same Introduction paragraph as 404 and referring to the same Dutch translation. Cite drift only: printed p.4, not p.3.

verdicts.trueWording: the virtue becomes unrecognisable for most Dutch readers
verdicts.note: Verbatim; the preceding clause is 'By preserving her name in the Dutch translation', and the two sentences before it establish 'her' as Lady Patience, the only character whose royal status makes her name indicate a virtue. Cite drift only: printed p.12, not p.11; section 5 is correct.

verdicts.trueWording: most likely to clarify the virtue associated with King Shrewd
verdicts.note: Verbatim; the added-information limb is stated twice, 'extra information is added in the Dutch translation' and 'Feberwee and Cuijpers choose to add some information' (Koning Vlijm de Listige for Koning Vlijm). Cite drift: p.13 is right but that page is section 5, Translation criticism - Proper names (pp.10-13); section 6 starts at p.14.

verdicts.trueWording: Een geschiedenis van de Zes Hertogdommen is noodzakelijkerwijs een geschiedenis
verdicts.note: Verbatim as the opening line of section 7 on printed p.19, under Duits's heading 'De Vroegste Geschiedenis', continuing 'van zijn heersers, de Zieners' — i.e. of its rulers, the Farseers. Appendix A confirms the source text is the novel's opening 'The Earliest History' epigraph (listed as Passage 1: page 1-4), so 'first epigraph' is right; note her passage 1 runs on past the epigraph into the main text.

verdicts.trueWording: excerpts from a public document, largely a formal history
verdicts.note: Raw PDF via the Wayback capture named in the routeHint (21pp). Verbatim on printed p.45, of 'The chapter epigraphs'; the same page states each chapter begins with a lengthy epigraph selected from a history of the Six Duchies. Page cite correct.

verdicts.trueWording: written in a distant, scholarly voice
verdicts.note: Verbatim on printed p.45, the tail of the same sentence as 409, modifying the formal history the chapter epigraphs excerpt. Page cite correct. Oliver frames the voice as in-world Fitz's; attributing the epigraphs to Hobb is the outer authorial frame and does not disturb the characterisation.

verdicts.trueWording: the dry, impersonal, but objective history beginning the chapter
verdicts.note: Verbatim on printed p.57, immediately before the NEGATIVE NARRATION heading. Both limbs hold: the full sentence says the marginalia, that is, the main text, feels more authoritative and satisfying than that history. Nuance for downstream: the sentence is local to the Lady Patience chapter, and Oliver keeps 'but objective' in the descriptor, which the claim drops.

verdicts.trueWording: whereas in the earlier epigraphs Fitz has largely kept the style
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim on printed p.62 (twelve-word cap forces the trim; the sentence continues 'of the epigraphs and the main text separate, here a poetic lyricism creeps into his style in the epigraph'). Chapter 15 limb holds: Oliver locates the blur at the start of the 'misted' section in chapter 15. Two hedges the claim drops — Oliver says 'largely kept', and calls chapter 15 the best example of the blurring rather than its only instance, having already noted ornate style seeping into the 'vision' description.

verdicts.trueWording: sentences that start by telling what a character is not doing
verdicts.note: Verbatim on printed p.57 under the NEGATIVE NARRATION heading; the source continues 'or feeling', and the claim's 'repeatedly' is carried by the surrounding 'continual insistence' and 'particularly frequent in the early chapters'. Oliver's own coinage for the device is 'negative narration'.

verdicts.trueWording: scarcely a page goes by without obvious examples
verdicts.note: Verbatim on printed p.57, in the clause 'This is particularly frequent in the early chapters, where...', so the early-chapters limb holds. Oliver then lists three instances from pp.6, 7 and 9 of the novel. Note the kind field says 'measurement': this is an impressionistic frequency claim, not a count.

verdicts.trueWording: Robin a un style très fluide, très clair et très imagé
verdicts.note: Live page fetched directly with a browser user agent; byline 'Jérôme Vincent - le 31/10/2017' and the question 'Comment définiriez-vous son style ?' both present as cited. The answer continues 'sous des apparences simples', supporting 'beneath simple appearances'. Translator limb confirmed on the same page: ActuSF says he worked on novels by Card, Robin Hobb, Moorcock and Silverberg, and he speaks as a translator ('je traduis... pour l'Atalante').
